Investigate the relationship between the structure of digit modules and subsets found by methods like 'and mask' under more domains.
papers.abstract: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? Peters et al. (2016) provides a positive answer for linear cases. In this paper, we use a functional modular probing method to analyze deep model structures under OOD setting. We demonstrate that even in biased models (which focus on spurious correlation) there still exist unbiased functional subnetworks. Furthermore, we articulate and demonstrate the functional lottery ticket hypothesis: full network contains a subnetwork that can achieve better OOD performance. We then propose Modular Risk Minimization to solve the subnetwork selection problem. Our algorithm learns the subnetwork structure from a given dataset, and can be combined with any other OOD regularization methods. Experiments on various OOD generalization tasks corroborate the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Interpreting Adversarial Examples by Activation Promotion and Suppression
papers.research_question: How to interpret the mechanism of adversarial perturbations at pixel, image, and network levels, and how does this interpretability help improve robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to interpret adversarial examples by revealing the promotion-suppression effect (PSE) on neurons' activations, linking pixel-level perturbations to discriminative image regions via CAM, and connecting unit sensitivity to concept interpretability via network dissection.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive interpretation of adversarial examples at pixel, image, and network levels, showing that adversarial attacks induce activation promotion and suppression effects linked to discriminative regions and unit interpretability, offering insights for improving robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial perturbations exhibit a promotion-suppression effect (PSE) and can be categorized into suppression-dominated, promotion-dominated, and balanced types.
Pixel-level adversarial perturbations are strongly associated with class-specific discriminative image regions localized by class activation mapping (CAM).
There is a tight connection between the sensitivity of hidden units to adversarial perturbations and their interpretability on semantic concepts, as revealed by network dissection.
The interpretability of adversarial patterns constrains the effectiveness of adversarial attacks; refining attacks by focusing on high-sensitivity pixels can maintain success with fewer perturbations.
Neuron masking based on sensitivity and interpretability can improve adversarial robustness at a slight cost to clean accuracy.
future_direction: Develop interpretability-driven defensive methods and consider attacks against interpretability, not just prediction.
papers.abstract: It is widely known that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial examples: images with imperceptible perturbations crafted to fool classifiers. However, interpretability of these perturbations is less explored in the literature. This work aims to better understand the roles of adversarial perturbations and provide visual explanations from pixel, image and network perspectives. We show that adversaries have a promotion-suppression effect (PSE) on neurons' activations and can be primarily categorized into three types: i) suppression-dominated perturbations that mainly reduce the classification score of the true label, ii) promotion-dominated perturbations that focus on boosting the confidence of the target label, and iii) balanced perturbations that play a dual role in suppression and promotion. We also provide image-level interpretability of adversarial examples. This links PSE of pixel-level perturbations to class-specific discriminative image regions localized by class activation mapping (Zhou et al. 2016). Further, we examine the adversarial effect through network dissection (Bau et al. 2017), which offers concept-level interpretability of hidden units. We show that there exists a tight connection between the units' sensitivity to adversarial attacks and their interpretability on semantic concepts. Lastly, we provide some new insights from our interpretation to improve the adversarial robustness of networks.

papers.title: Explaining the Explainer: Understanding the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Symbolic Regression Models
papers.research_question: How can we understand the internal mechanisms of transformer-based symbolic regression models, specifically by identifying circuits responsible for generating symbolic operators?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PATCHES, a novel evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm for symbolic regression transformers, and establishes a formal evaluation framework (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) for circuit correctness.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes symbolic regression as a promising domain for mechanistic interpretability and provides a principled methodology for circuit discovery in such models.
papers.key_findings:
PATCHES successfully isolates circuits for specific symbolic operators (e.g., sin, add, log) in a transformer-based SR model.
Mean patching combined with functional evaluation (accuracy) is more reliable for discovering correct circuits than resample patching or model-based (logit) evaluation.
Direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features, limiting their utility for causal circuit discovery.
Circuits for SR are dense (40-78% of model components), attributed to the small vocabulary and complex syntactic encoding required.
papers.limitation:
Resample patching sometimes fails to sufficiently suppress the target token's information, hindering causal isolation and circuit discovery.
High baseline performance for some operators (e.g., addition) makes it difficult to achieve completeness, as patching does not degrade performance enough.
papers.abstract: Following their success across many domains, transformers have also proven effective for symbolic regression (SR); however, the internal mechanisms underlying their generation of mathematical operators remain largely unexplored. Although mechanistic interpretability has successfully identified circuits in language and vision models, it has not yet been applied to SR. In this article, we introduce PATCHES, an evolutionary circuit discovery algorithm that identifies compact and correct circuits for SR. Using PATCHES, we isolate 28 circuits, providing the first circuit-level characterisation of an SR transformer. We validate these findings through a robust causal evaluation framework based on key notions such as faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. Our analysis shows that mean patching with performance-based evaluation most reliably isolates functionally correct circuits. In contrast, we demonstrate that direct logit attribution and probing classifiers primarily capture correlational features rather than causal ones, limiting their utility for circuit discovery. Overall, these results establish SR as a high-potential application domain for mechanistic interpretability and propose a principled methodology for circuit discovery.

papers.title: Emergence of Minimal Circuits for Indirect Object Identification in Attention-Only Transformers
papers.research_question: How do minimal circuits for indirect object identification emerge in attention-only transformers trained from scratch on a symbolic task?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that task-constrained training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits for indirect object identification in attention-only transformers.
papers.conclusion: Task-constrained training can produce parsimonious and interpretable circuits, offering insight into computational motifs underlying reasoning in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A single-layer, two-head attention-only transformer achieves perfect accuracy on the symbolic IOI task.
The two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution.
A two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance through composition across layers via query-value interactions.
Positional embeddings improve accuracy and interpretability but are not strictly necessary for the task.
The circuits in task-constrained models are more parsimonious than those in broadly pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer large language models (LLMs) into human-understandable computational circuits. However, the complexity of pretrained models often obscures the minimal mechanisms required for specific reasoning tasks. In this work, we train small, attention-only transformers from scratch on a symbolic version of the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task -- a benchmark for studying coreference -- like reasoning in transformers. Surprisingly, a single-layer model with only two attention heads achieves perfect IOI accuracy, despite lacking MLPs and normalization layers. Through residual stream decomposition, spectral analysis, and embedding interventions, we find that the two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution. Furthermore, we show that a two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance by composing information across layers through query-value interactions. These results demonstrate that task-specific training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits, offering a controlled testbed for probing the computational foundations of transformer reasoning.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: Natural language instructions induce compositional generalization in networks of neurons
papers.research_question: What neural computations allow networks to interpret linguistic instructions and perform novel tasks without explicit experience?
papers.core_contribution: Language instructions enable zero-shot generalization in neural networks by aligning sensorimotor representations with the semantic geometry of instructions, allowing composition of practiced skills for novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how linguistic instructions induce compositional generalization in neural networks, offering testable predictions for neural representations underlying flexible cognition in the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Models using sentence-level semantics (e.g., SBERT) achieve up to 83% correct zero-shot generalization on unseen tasks.
Language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that their geometry shares structure with instruction embeddings, facilitating compositionality.
Individual neurons in the sensorimotor network modulate their tuning based on the semantics of instructions.
The network can produce linguistic descriptions of novel tasks based solely on motor feedback, enabling knowledge transfer to partner models.
Generalization is supported by cross-condition generalization performance (CCGP) metrics that correlate with task performance.
future_direction: Guiding imaging studies to delineate brain areas involved in instruction following
Comparing compositional representations in nonlinguistic subjects like nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: A fundamental human cognitive feat is to interpret linguistic instructions in order to perform novel tasks without explicit task experience. Yet, the neural computations that might be used to accomplish this remain poorly understood. We use advances in natural language processing to create a neural model of generalization based on linguistic instructions. Models are trained on a set of common psychophysical tasks, and receive instructions embedded by a pretrained language model. Our best models can perform a previously unseen task with an average performance of 83% correct based solely on linguistic instructions (that is, zero-shot learning). We found that language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that activity for interrelated tasks shares a common geometry with the semantic representations of instructions, allowing language to cue the proper composition of practiced skills in unseen settings. We show how this model generates a linguistic description of a novel task it has identified using only motor feedback, which can subsequently guide a partner model to perform the task. Our models offer several experimentally testable predictions outlining how linguistic information must be represented to facilitate flexible and general cognition in the human brain.

papers.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: How can we rigorously evaluate the faithfulness of natural language explanations that claim individual neurons in a language model represent a concept?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework with observational and intervention modes to evaluate natural language explanations of neurons, and applies it to show that GPT-4-generated explanations for GPT-2 XL neurons have low faithfulness and causal efficacy.
papers.conclusion: Natural language may not be the best medium for model explanations due to vagueness and ambiguity, and neurons may not be the optimal unit of analysis; structured formalisms and analysis of neuron groups are promising alternatives.
papers.key_findings:
Even among the top 0.6% of neurons with GPT-4 explanation scores ≥0.8, explanations achieve only 0.64 precision and 0.50 recall.
Intervention-based evaluation shows GPT-4 explanations have little to no causal efficacy, performing similarly to random baselines.
Individual neurons are not effective causal mediators; causal effects require aggregating over many neurons, especially in early MLP layers.
Natural language explanations are often vague and ambiguous, making them unreliable for technical decision-making.
The GPT-4 score used by Bills et al. (2023) is insensitive to Type I errors and does not guarantee faithful explanations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on GPT-2 XL; results may not extend directly to other architectures.
Faithful explanations could be used for malicious manipulations of models.
future_direction: Use structured formalisms (e.g., programming languages) instead of natural language for explanations.
Analyze groups of neurons or other network components (e.g., attention heads, residual streams) as units of analysis.
Conduct similar evaluations on other model architectures.
papers.abstract: Natural language is an appealing medium for explaining how large language models process and store information, but evaluating the faithfulness of such explanations is challenging. To help address this, we develop two modes of evaluation for natural language explanations that claim individual neurons represent a concept in a text input. In the *observational mode*, we evaluate claims that a neuron a activates on all and only input strings that refer to a concept picked out by the proposed explanation E. In the *intervention mode*, we construe E as a claim that neuron a is a causal mediator of the concept denoted by E. We apply our framework to the GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons of Bills et al. (2023) and show that even the most confident explanations have high error rates and little to no causal efficacy. We close the paper by critically assessing whether natural language is a good choice for explanations and whether neurons are the best level of analysis.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: The Stem Cell Hypothesis: Dilemma behind Multi-Task Learning with Transformer Encoders
papers.research_question: Why does multi-task learning (MTL) with transformer encoders on distinct core NLP tasks lead to worse performance than single-task learning, and is there a subset of attention heads that are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for all?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Stem Cell Hypothesis, which states that a subset of attention heads (stem cells) are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks, leading to interference and worse performance in multi-task learning.
papers.conclusion: The Stem Cell Hypothesis sheds light on the dilemma of multi-task learning with transformer encoders, indicating that attention heads cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks without interference, and suggests a direction for future MTL research by wisely assigning heads to tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-task learning on five core NLP tasks (POS, NER, DEP, CON, SRL) results in lower performance than single-task learning for all tasks.
Pruning analysis reveals that all five tasks rely on a similar set of attention heads, primarily in middle layers (5-8), which are termed 'stem cells'.
Even without fine-tuning, certain attention heads (stem cells) show high probing accuracy for specific linguistic labels, demonstrating their pluripotency.
During single-task learning, stem cells become specialized for the task, but during multi-task learning, they lose specialization due to conflicting training signals.
The Stem Cell Hypothesis is validated by novel parameter-free probes that show how attention heads are transformed during training, with MTL often degrading probing and task performance.
future_direction: Adapt the work to more tasks and languages for broader generality.
Design another probing method for deeper analysis in constituency parsing (CON).
papers.abstract: Multi-task learning with transformer encoders (MTL) has emerged as a powerful technique to improve performance on closely-related tasks for both accuracy and efficiency while a question still remains whether or not it would perform as well on tasks that are distinct in nature. We first present MTL results on five NLP tasks, POS, NER, DEP, CON, and SRL, and depict its deficiency over single-task learning. We then conduct an extensive pruning analysis to show that a certain set of attention heads get claimed by most tasks during MTL, who interfere with one another to fine-tune those heads for their own objectives. Based on this finding, we propose the Stem Cell Hypothesis to reveal the existence of attention heads naturally talented for many tasks that cannot be jointly trained to create adequate embeddings for all of those tasks. Finally, we design novel parameter-free probes to justify our hypothesis and demonstrate how attention heads are transformed across the five tasks during MTL through label analysis. papers.title: Uncovering mesa-optimization algorithms in Transformers
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning emerge in autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction? The paper investigates whether such training gives rise to a gradient-based optimization algorithm (mesa-optimizer) that adjusts the model as new inputs are revealed.
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction learn a gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithm that performs in-context learning, explaining the emergence of in-context learning and inspiring new Transformer layers.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in autoregressive Transformers arises from mesa-optimization algorithms learned during training, which can be leveraged to design more efficient optimization-based layers.
papers.key_findings:
Early Transformer layers learn a token binding mechanism that aggregates consecutive observations into internal representations, enabling subsequent mesa-optimization.
Trained single-layer linear self-attention models implement one-step gradient descent on a least-squares objective, matching the theoretical construction.
Multi-layer linear self-attention models implement a preconditioned gradient descent algorithm that approximates the optimal least-squares solution.
The proposed mesa-layer, derived from optimization principles, performs recursive least squares and improves language modeling performance compared to standard linear attention.
Standard softmax Transformers trained on synthetic sequence tasks exhibit internal activation patterns consistent with mesa-optimization across layers.
papers.limitation: The language modeling results are not sufficient to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers; more reverse-engineering is needed.
future_direction: Studying the mesa-layer equipped with forgetting factors
More reverse-engineering work to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers
Designing new optimization-based Transformer layers
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant model in deep learning, but the reason for their superior performance is poorly understood. Here, we hypothesize that the strong performance of Transformers stems from an architectural bias towards mesa-optimization, a learned process running within the forward pass of a model consisting of the following two steps: (i) the construction of an internal learning objective, and (ii) its corresponding solution found through optimization. To test this hypothesis, we reverse-engineer a series of autoregressive Transformers trained on simple sequence modeling tasks, uncovering underlying gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithms driving the generation of predictions. Moreover, we show that the learned forward-pass optimization algorithm can be immediately repurposed to solve supervised few-shot tasks, suggesting that mesa-optimization might underlie the in-context learning capabilities of large language models. Finally, we propose a novel self-attention layer, the mesa-layer, that explicitly and efficiently solves optimization problems specified in context. We find that this layer can lead to improved performance in synthetic and preliminary language modeling experiments, adding weight to our hypothesis that mesa-optimization is an important operation hidden within the weights of trained Transformers.

papers.title: Do VLMs Have Bad Eyes? Diagnosing Compositional Failures via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Are entangled or misaligned representations within the CLIP vision encoder the root cause for failures in compositional reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that superposition (entanglement of multiple features in individual neurons) in CLIP's vision encoder is a root cause of failures in compositional reasoning and object binding.
papers.conclusion: The study establishes superposition as a key bottleneck for object-attribute compositionality and motivates future work on disentangling neuron activations to improve CLIP's feature representation.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neurons in CLIP's MLP layers represent multiple features (superposition), which hinders compositional feature representation.
Grad-CAM visualizations show that CLIP fails to bind attributes to objects, attending to multiple unrelated regions when the full conjunction is missing.
Using entropy, the paper identifies feature-selective neurons in CLIP's MLP layers that respond to specific visual attributes.
The paper provides evidence of superposition in neurons, showing that the same neuron can activate for multiple distinct features (e.g., circle and square).
Superposition is correlated with reduced separability in embedding space (smaller cluster-center distance) and higher misclassification rates on compositional tasks.
papers.limitation: This study is limited to the CLIP-ViT-L/14 model, whereas most modern vision-language models (VLMs) adopt variants such as SigLIP and alternative architectures like SAM.
future_direction: Extending analysis to other models like SigLIP and SAM.
Establishing a more direct causal link between weak compositional feature representations and failures in compositional reasoning.
Extending analysis to more complex, feature-annotated datasets.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable performance in integrating visual and textual information for tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering. However, these models struggle with compositional generalization and object binding, which limit their ability to handle novel combinations of objects and their attributes. Our work explores the root causes of these failures using mechanistic interpretability techniques. We show evidence that individual neurons in the MLP layers of CLIP's vision encoder represent multiple features, and this "superposition" directly hinders its compositional feature representation which consequently affects compositional reasoning and object binding capabilities. We hope this study will serve as an initial step toward uncovering the mechanistic roots of compositional failures in VLMs. The code and supporting results can be found https://github.com/Mystic-Slice/Do-VLMs-Have-Bad-Eyes.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis
papers.research_question: What is the stability of mechanistic interpretability methods, specifically circuit discovery, and how does variance in causal mediation analysis and its approximations affect the reliability of discovered circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that circuit discovery methods are highly unstable due to intrinsic variance in causal mediation analysis scores and amplification by approximation methods, advocating for more rigorous statistical practices in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Circuit discovery is not a stable process and requires statistical rigor, including reporting stability metrics and sensitivity analyses, to become a reliable scientific tool.
papers.key_findings:
Exact causal mediation analysis (CMA) scores exhibit high intrinsic variance across inputs, meaning the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable.
Approximation methods like Edge Attribution Patching (EAP) amplify this variance, leading to low signal-to-noise ratios.
Circuit discovery pipelines are sensitive to data resampling, hyperparameters, and counterfactual definitions, resulting in structurally inconsistent circuits.
Larger models (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B) show higher variability in circuit discovery compared to smaller models (e.g., gpt2-small).
The instability of circuits is not mitigated by instruction tuning (comparing Llama-3.2-1B and its instruct variant).
papers.limitation:
Focus on the EAP family of methods, leaving out newer methods that may have different properties.
Exact CMA analysis was only done on gpt2-small for the IOI task due to computational constraints.
Limited to three classic MI tasks, which may not generalize to fuzzier reasoning tasks.
Stability metrics treat all edges equally, whereas weighted metrics might reveal a stable functional core.
future_direction: Probabilistic circuit discovery: characterizing a distribution over possible circuits.
Decomposing variance into estimator variance and intrinsic variance.
Stability-aware optimization: developing objectives that explicitly optimize for stability.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer model behaviors by identifying functional sub-networks. Yet, the scientific validity of these findings depends on their stability. In this work, we argue that circuit discovery is not a standalone task but a statistical estimation problem built upon causal mediation analysis (CMA). We uncover a fundamental instability at this base layer: exact, single-input CMA scores exhibit high intrinsic variance, implying that the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable rather than a fixed property. We then demonstrate that circuit discovery pipelines inherit this variance and further amplify it. Fast approximation methods, such as Edge Attribution Patching and its successors, introduce additional estimation noise, while aggregating these noisy scores over datasets leads to fragile structural estimates. Consequently, small perturbations in input data or hyperparameters yield vastly different circuits. We systematically decompose these sources of variance and advocate for more rigorous MI practices, prioritizing statistical robustness and routine reporting of stability metrics.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Linguistic Interpretability of Transformer-based Language Models: a systematic review
papers.research_question: What linguistic knowledge do Transformer-based language models encode internally, and how is it represented across different linguistic levels like syntax, morphology, lexico-semantics, and discourse?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive analysis and unified vision of linguistic interpretability in Transformer-based pre-trained language models, reviewing 160 works across multiple languages and linguistic levels.
papers.conclusion: The survey fills a gap in interpretability literature by synthesizing findings on linguistic knowledge in PLMs, highlighting variability and ongoing debates.
papers.key_findings:
There is no consensus on the layerwise location of syntactic information in PLMs, with studies reporting different layers for different phenomena.
Semantic information is often encoded in middle to higher layers, but this varies across languages and models.
Morphological information is frequently studied alongside syntax or semantics, and tokenization schemes can hinder its analysis.
Discourse information is less explored, but some works indicate that PLMs can encode discourse structure.
The geometry of contextualized embeddings shows separate subspaces for syntactic and semantic information.
papers.abstract: Language models based on the Transformer architecture achieve excellent results in many language-related tasks, such as text classification or sentiment analysis. However, despite the architecture of these models being well-defined, little is known about how their internal computations help them achieve their results. This renders these models, as of today, a type of 'black box' systems. There is, however, a line of research -- 'interpretability' -- aiming to learn how information is encoded inside these models. More specifically, there is work dedicated to studying whether Transformer-based models possess knowledge of linguistic phenomena similar to human speakers -- an area we call 'linguistic interpretability' of these models. In this survey we present a comprehensive analysis of 160 research works, spread across multiple languages and models -- including multilingual ones -- that attempt to discover linguistic information from the perspective of several traditional Linguistics disciplines: Syntax, Morphology, Lexico-Semantics and Discourse. Our survey fills a gap in the existing interpretability literature, which either not focus on linguistic knowledge in these models or present some limitations -- e.g. only studying English-based models. Our survey also focuses on Pre-trained Language Models not further specialized for a downstream task, with an emphasis on works that use interpretability techniques that explore models' internal representations.

papers.title: Decomposing Language Models Into Understandable Components
papers.research_question: How can we decompose language models into interpretable components to understand their behavior, moving beyond individual neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using dictionary learning to decompose language models into interpretable features, which are more understandable than individual neurons and enable targeted steering of model behavior.
papers.conclusion: This decomposition method moves past the roadblock of uninterpretable neurons, potentially enabling monitoring and steering of model behavior for improved safety and reliability. The next challenge is scaling the approach to larger frontier models.
papers.key_findings:
Features are significantly more interpretable than neurons, as validated by blinded human evaluator scores.
Features allow for targeted steering of model behavior, causing predictable changes when artificially activated.
The learned features are largely universal between different models.
Varying the number of features provides a control for the resolution of model interpretation, from coarse to refined views.
This approach overcomes the roadblock of uninterpretable neurons in mechanistic understanding.
papers.limitation: The method is demonstrated on a small model and scaling to larger frontier models is an engineering obstacle.
future_direction: Scaling the approach up to frontier models which are larger and more complicated.
papers.abstract: How can we decompose language models into interpretable components to understand their behavior, moving beyond individual neurons? Introduces a method using dictionary learning to decompose language models into interpretable features, which are more understandable than individual neurons and enable targeted steering of model behavior. This decomposition method moves past the roadblock of uninterpretable neurons, potentially enabling monitoring and steering of model behavior for improved safety and reliability. The next challenge is scaling the approach to larger frontier models.

papers.title: DeepDecipher: Accessing and Investigating Neuron Activation in Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces DeepDecipher, an API and interface for probing neurons in transformer models' MLP layers, making advanced interpretability techniques more accessible.
papers.conclusion: DeepDecipher provides a user-friendly way to understand how neurons in Transformer and MLP layers work, aiming to make complex AI systems easier to explain and more secure.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability for practical usage in safety monitoring of large language models is limited by the large number of neurons in state-of-the-art LLMs and the difficulty in reverse-engineering the learned functions.
All three integrated methods rely on max activating examples, and the neurons' behaviour here may not be representative of its behaviour in general.
The usability of DeepDecipher in practice is currently broadly untested due to time constraints.
future_direction: Redesigning parts of the user interface.
Ensuring support for proprietary models.
Implementing better search functionality and partnering with researchers to provide a comprehensive database of models.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more capable, there is an urgent need for interpretable and transparent tools. Current methods are difficult to implement, and accessible tools to analyze model internals are lacking. To bridge this gap, we present DeepDecipher - an API and interface for probing neurons in transformer models' MLP layers. DeepDecipher makes the outputs of advanced interpretability techniques for LLMs readily available. The easy-to-use interface also makes inspecting these complex models more intuitive. This paper outlines DeepDecipher's design and capabilities. We demonstrate how to analyze neurons, compare models, and gain insights into model behavior. For example, we contrast DeepDecipher's functionality with similar tools like Neuroscope and OpenAI's Neuron Explainer. DeepDecipher enables efficient, scalable analysis of LLMs. By granting access to state-of-the-art interpretability methods, DeepDecipher makes LLMs more transparent, trustworthy, and safe. Researchers, engineers, and developers can quickly diagnose issues, audit systems, and advance the field.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.

papers.title: What's in the Image? A Deep-Dive into the Vision of Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Vision-Language Models process visual information and what is the information flow between visual and textual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that VLMs compress high-level image information into query tokens, that middle layers are critical for cross-modal information flow, and that fine-grained details are retrieved from image tokens in a spatially localized manner. It also proposes new evaluation protocols and demonstrates an application for efficient visual processing.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers novel insights about VLM internal visual representation and processing, with two core mechanisms: visual information compression into text tokens and spatially-aware retrieval of fine details. It introduces new evaluation methods and the Image Re-prompting application for efficient multi-question answering.
papers.key_findings:
Query tokens act as global image descriptors, storing compressed high-level image information.
Middle layers (approx 25% of layers) are crucial for vision-to-language transfer, while early and late layers contribute marginally.
Fine-grained visual attributes are directly retrieved from image tokens in a spatially localized manner.
The proposed LLM-based evaluation protocol effectively compares free-text descriptions.
Image Re-prompting allows efficient multi-question answering with compressed context.
future_direction: Extend analysis to multi-image and video, expanding Image Re-prompting to expand VLMs effective visual context windows.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in comprehending complex visual content. However, the mechanisms underlying how VLMs process visual information remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we conduct a thorough empirical analysis, focusing on attention modules across layers. We reveal several key insights about how these models process visual data: (i) the internal representation of the query tokens (e.g., representations of "describe the image"), is utilized by VLMs to store global image information; we demonstrate that these models generate surprisingly descriptive responses solely from these tokens, without direct access to image tokens. (ii) Cross-modal information flow is predominantly influenced by the middle layers (approximately 25% of all layers), while early and late layers contribute only marginally.(iii) Fine-grained visual attributes and object details are directly extracted from image tokens in a spatially localized manner, i.e., the generated tokens associated with a specific object or attribute attend strongly to their corresponding regions in the image. We propose novel quantitative evaluation to validate our observations, leveraging real-world complex visual scenes. Finally, we demonstrate the potential of our findings in facilitating efficient visual processing in state-of-the-art VLMs.

papers.title: Priors in Time: Missing Inductive Biases for Language Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the temporal prior assumptions of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and how do they conflict with the actual temporal structure in language model activations? How can we design an interpretability method that incorporates appropriate temporal inductive biases?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Feature Analysis, a new interpretability protocol that decomposes language model activations into predictable (contextual) and novel (residual) components, capturing temporal structure that standard Sparse Autoencoders miss due to inappropriate inductive biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability tools must incorporate inductive biases that match the data's structure, and Temporal Feature Analysis offers a promising direction for capturing temporal dynamics in language model representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs impose an i.i.d. prior over time, assuming concepts are independent across time, which conflicts with the non-stationary temporal structure (e.g., increasing intrinsic dimensionality, context correlations) observed in language model activations.
Temporal Feature Analysis successfully decomposes activations into predictable (slow-moving, contextual) and novel (fast-moving, stimulus-driven) components, aligning with the generative structure of language.
The predictive component of Temporal Feature Analysis captures smooth temporal trajectories, event boundaries, and speaker roles in dialogue, while the novel component retains monosemantic features interpretable via standard autointerp pipelines.
In experiments on garden path sentences, stories, and in-context dialogue, Temporal Feature Analysis correctly parses linguistic structure and identifies event boundaries, whereas standard SAEs show significant pitfalls.
The method demonstrates that incorporating data-informed temporal inductive biases is crucial for robust interpretability tools.
papers.limitation: The method assumes that the residual novel component is i.i.d. over time, which may not hold in general.
future_direction: Explore other inductive biases (e.g., hierarchical, compositional) for interpretability.
Apply Temporal Feature Analysis to other modalities (e.g., video, audio).
Conduct more extensive causal intervention studies to validate the interpretability of the novel codes.
papers.abstract: Recovering meaningful concepts from language model activations is a central aim of interpretability. While existing feature extraction methods aim to identify concepts that are independent directions, it is unclear if this assumption can capture the rich temporal structure of language. Specifically, via a Bayesian lens, we demonstrate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) impose priors that assume independence of concepts across time, implying stationarity. Meanwhile, language model representations exhibit rich temporal dynamics, including systematic growth in conceptual dimensionality, context-dependent correlations, and pronounced non-stationarity, in direct conflict with the priors of SAEs. Taking inspiration from computational neuroscience, we introduce a new interpretability objective -- Temporal Feature Analysis -- which possesses a temporal inductive bias to decompose representations at a given time into two parts: a predictable component, which can be inferred from the context, and a residual component, which captures novel information unexplained by the context. Temporal Feature Analyzers correctly parse garden path sentences, identify event boundaries, and more broadly delineate abstract, slow-moving information from novel, fast-moving information, while existing SAEs show significant pitfalls in all the above tasks. Overall, our results underscore the need for inductive biases that match the data in designing robust interpretability tools.

papers.title: Why Linear Interpretability Works: Invariant Subspaces as a Result of Architectural Constraints
papers.research_question: Why do linear interpretability methods like linear probes and sparse autoencoders succeed in deep nonlinear transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear interpretability methods succeed because transformer architectures have linear communication interfaces (attention OV circuits and unembedding matrices), which force semantic features to occupy context-invariant linear subspaces. It introduces the Self-Reference Property, where tokens provide the geometric directions for their associated features, enabling zero-shot semantic classification.
papers.conclusion: Linear interpretability in transformers is a structural consequence of architectural constraints, not merely an empirical regularity. The Self-Reference Property enables zero-shot semantic classification without labeled data.
papers.key_findings:
The Invariant Subspace Necessity theorem establishes that any semantic feature decoded through a linear interface must lie in a context-invariant subspace.
The Self-Reference Property shows that tokens directly provide the invariant geometric directions for their associated features.
Empirical validation across eight classification tasks and four model families confirms that class tokens align with instance directions, supporting directional invariance.
Zero-shot, unsupervised, and sparse autoencoder-based probes all recover the same directional structure, providing converging evidence.
Polysemy (one token with multiple directions) and partial synonymy (multiple tokens sharing a direction) are two sides of the same coin in the geometric representation.
papers.limitation:
The framework focuses on features communicated through linear interfaces; features operating through nonlinear gating (e.g., QK routing) may not exhibit the same invariance.
The work does not characterize when invariant subspaces collapse to single directions versus higher-dimensional structures.
future_direction: The Self-Reference Property suggests paths toward scalable, unsupervised circuit discovery.
The connection between sparse autoencoder features and token directions offers new evaluation criteria for dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Linear probes and sparse autoencoders consistently recover meaningful structure from transformer representations -- yet why should such simple methods succeed in deep, nonlinear systems? We show this is not merely an empirical regularity but a consequence of architectural necessity: transformers communicate information through linear interfaces (attention OV circuits, unembedding matrices), and any semantic feature decoded through such an interface must occupy a context-invariant linear subspace. We formalize this as the \emph{Invariant Subspace Necessity} theorem and derive the \emph{Self-Reference Property}: tokens directly provide the geometric direction for their associated features, enabling zero-shot identification of semantic structure without labeled data or learned probes. Empirical validation in eight classification tasks and four model families confirms the alignment between class tokens and semantically related instances. Our framework provides \textbf{a principled architectural explanation} for why linear interpretability methods work, unifying linear probes and sparse autoencoders.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: TopK Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we build a language model architecture that enjoys the interpretability of sparse autoencoders without suffering the drawbacks of post-hoc training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TopK LMs, a transformer-based language model architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function to achieve inherent, SAE-like interpretability without requiring post-hoc training, while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: TopK LMs represent a significant advance toward trustworthy AI systems by making interpretability a built-in feature, demonstrating that performance and interpretability need not be competing objectives.
papers.key_findings:
TopK LMs achieve competitive language modeling and downstream task performance compared to dense baselines, with only a moderate increase in model size.
Neurons in TopK LMs exhibit higher concept specialization, as measured by lower token and semantic entropy, making them more interpretable.
Single-neuron interventions (activation patching) can causally steer the model's text generation towards specific concepts.
The formation and specialization of individual neurons can be traced continuously across training checkpoints and model layers.
Sparsity annealing during training improves convergence and model performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models up to ~1B parameters; effectiveness on significantly larger models remains an open question.
Evaluation focused on language modeling and standard reasoning benchmarks, leaving performance on specialized downstream tasks unclear.
Long-context modeling capabilities and the interaction between TopK sparsity and attention over long sequences were not examined.
The approach is currently limited to text-only models; extending to multimodal architectures requires future research.
Specific societal applications that could benefit from the model's interpretability were not explored.
future_direction: Scaling the TopK LM approach to significantly larger models (tens or hundreds of billions of parameters).
Extending TopK activation to multimodal architectures combining text with images, audio, or other modalities.
Investigating how TopK LMs can address concrete challenges in model alignment, fairness assessment, safety evaluation, and trustworthy AI deployment.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an important tool for analyzing and interpreting the activation space of transformer-based language models (LMs). However, SAEs suffer several shortcomings that diminish their utility and internal validity. Since SAEs are trained post-hoc, it is unclear if the failure to discover a particular concept is a failure on the SAE's side or due to the underlying LM not representing this concept. This problem is exacerbated by training conditions and architecture choices affecting which features an SAE learns. When tracing how LMs learn concepts during training, the lack of feature stability also makes it difficult to compare SAEs features across different checkpoints. To address these limitations, we introduce a modification to the transformer architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function at chosen layers, making the model's hidden states equivalent to the latent features of a TopK SAE. This approach eliminates the need for post-hoc training while providing interpretability comparable to SAEs. The resulting TopK LMs offer a favorable trade-off between model size, computational efficiency, and interpretability. Despite this simple architectural change, TopK LMs maintain their original capabilities while providing robust interpretability benefits. Our experiments demonstrate that the sparse representations learned by TopK LMs enable successful steering through targeted neuron interventions and facilitate detailed analysis of neuron formation processes across checkpoints and layers. These features make TopK LMs stable and reliable tools for understanding how language models learn and represent concepts, which we believe will significantly advance future research on model interpretability and controllability.

papers.title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
papers.research_question: How universal are circuits across different languages? Specifically, does Gemma 2B implement similar circuits for solving the subject-verb agreement task in English and Spanish?
papers.core_contribution: The circuits for subject-verb agreement in Gemma 2B are highly consistent across English and Spanish, driven by an attention head that writes a language-independent subject number signal to the residual stream, which is read by specific MLP neurons to promote the correct verb form.
papers.conclusion: Through activation patching and direct logit attribution we find that both languages rely on circuits that are highly consistent. Moreover, we provide evidence of an attention head (L13H7) writing a ‘subject number’ signal as a direction from which downstream neurons read to promote the correct verb number continuation. Finally, we show this direction has a causal effect, being able to flip the predicted verb number across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The English and Spanish circuits for subject-verb agreement in Gemma 2B are highly consistent.
The circuit is mainly driven by attention head L13H7 writing a subject number signal to the residual stream.
Downstream neurons in MLP13 (e.g., neuron 2069) read this signal to promote the correct verb number.
The subject number signal is represented as a direction in the residual stream space (PC1) and is language-independent.
Activation steering using the English-derived direction can flip the verb number prediction in Spanish.
papers.limitation:
The study focused solely on Gemma 2B model, so results may not generalize to other models.
The study is limited to two languages (English and Spanish), so the findings may not apply to all languages, especially linguistically distant ones.

papers.title: Understanding polysemanticity in neural networks through coding theory
papers.research_question: How can coding theory and eigenspectrum analysis provide insights into polysemanticity and improve interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a coding theory perspective to neural network interpretability, using eigenspectrum analysis of activation covariance and random projections to understand polysemanticity, redundancy, and the trade-off between capacity and robustness in network codes.
papers.conclusion: The eigenspectrum analysis and random projections offer a top-down perspective on neural network interpretability, advancing understanding of code structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks learn codes that balance capacity and redundancy, with eigenspectrum decay indicating the level of redundancy.
Dropout during training leads to faster eigenspectrum decay, more robust codes, and smoother random projections.
Random projections of hidden activations reveal the smoothness of the code, which is linked to eigenspectrum decay and can complement single-neuron interpretability methods.
In large language models, random projections provide explanatory power in layers where single-neuron methods perform poorly, suggesting complementary approaches.
The framework explains polysemanticity as an efficient encoding strategy and provides theoretical insights into optimal coding and error correction.
papers.limitation: Identifying the exact error-correcting code is beyond the scope of this paper.
future_direction: A systematic study of how eigenspectrum decay changes with network size.
Investigating the role of nonlinearities in the network code.
Further research into the underlying structure and behavior of deep learning models from a coding perspective.
papers.abstract: Despite substantial efforts, neural network interpretability remains an elusive goal, with previous research failing to provide succinct explanations of most single neurons' impact on the network output. This limitation is due to the polysemantic nature of most neurons, whereby a given neuron is involved in multiple unrelated network states, complicating the interpretation of that neuron. In this paper, we apply tools developed in neuroscience and information theory to propose both a novel practical approach to network interpretability and theoretical insights into polysemanticity and the density of codes. We infer levels of redundancy in the network's code by inspecting the eigenspectrum of the activation's covariance matrix. Furthermore, we show how random projections can reveal whether a network exhibits a smooth or non-differentiable code and hence how interpretable the code is. This same framework explains the advantages of polysemantic neurons to learning performance and explains trends found in recent results by Elhage et al.~(2022). Our approach advances the pursuit of interpretability in neural networks, providing insights into their underlying structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.

papers.title: Prisma: An Open Source Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability in Vision and Video
papers.core_contribution: Prisma is an open-source toolkit for vision mechanistic interpretability that provides hooked vision transformers, sparse autoencoder training and evaluation, circuit analysis tools, and educational resources. The paper also presents initial findings on vision SAEs, showing they are less sparse than language SAEs and can sometimes improve model loss when used in the forward pass.
papers.conclusion: Prisma bridges language and vision interpretability techniques with an extensive toolkit including 80+ SAEs for CLIP, DINO, and video transformers, and experimental toy models. The analysis reveals vision representations are less sparse than language models, and SAE reconstructions can improve model performance, especially for CLS tokens in deeper layers.
papers.key_findings:
Vision SAEs exhibit significantly higher sparsity (L0) than language SAEs, which may be due to information density differences, patch granularity, patch type specialization, or domain-specific optimization.
Injecting SAE reconstructions into the forward pass can sometimes decrease the original model's cross-entropy loss, especially for CLS tokens in deeper layers, suggesting a potential denoising mechanism.
